tagline: A freeway through wooded hills, with trains sharing the corridor.
intro: East of the Caldecott Tunnel, Route 24 runs through wooded hillsides and suburbs in Contra Costa County. It is a freeway throughout, with BART trains in the median except near the tunnel and the approach to Interstate 680. Caltrans has designated the stretch from the tunnel’s eastern end to I-680 as a scenic highway.

The road’s passage through the hills took decades to secure: an 1871 private tunneling attempt led by L.W. Kennedy struck water after about 200 feet and washed out. Alameda and Contra Costa counties formed Joint Highway District 13 in 1929 to replace the inadequate existing tunnel. Highway 24 received its number in 1932 while the new tunnel was under construction. The new twin bores opened in 1937. They were originally called the Broadway Low Level Tunnel, below the older Inter-County Tunnel’s portal. By 1960, a freeway eastern approach had helped accelerate Contra Costa County’s change from agricultural community to major suburb.

From the east portal, the highway crosses unincorporated land before entering Orinda. Rolling, oak-covered hills frame the city. Continue east into Lafayette, where the freeway crosses the Mokelumne Aqueduct soon after entering town. The drive ends at I-680 just inside Walnut Creek, where Route 24 itself terminates.
notice: BART tracks occupy the freeway median, except near the Caldecott Tunnel and the I-680 approach.

moments.title: Caldecott Tunnel
moments.text: The two oldest Caldecott bores carry eastbound traffic; the newer pair carries westbound traffic. That arrangement replaced a daily balancing act. After the third bore opened in 1964, the middle bore could reverse direction to give commuters four lanes in the heavier direction. Plastic lane markers rose from tubes in the pavement when filled with water, helping separate traffic. The fourth bore, completed in 2013, ended that daily reversal. The tunnel bears the name of Thomas E. Caldecott, a former Berkeley mayor and president of the highway district that built the first pair.

moments.title: Orinda
moments.text: Orinda’s oak-covered hills once held a rural landscape known for ranching and summer cabins. In 1876, County Sheriff William Walker Camron bought land east of the Berkeley Hills and named it Orinda Park. His wife, Alice Marsh Camron, admired Katherine Philips, the poet known as the Matchless Orinda. Year-round residence became more popular after the Caldecott opened in 1937 and eased travel west. BART service reached Orinda in 1973, after completion of its separate Berkeley Hills Tunnel. Its island platform sits in Route 24’s median. An abstract mural by Win Ng occupies the station’s fare lobby.

moments.title: Lafayette
moments.text: Lafayette’s name followed a rejected first choice for its post office. In 1857, Benjamin Shreve proposed Centerville, then suggested La Fayette after learning that California already had a post office with his first choice. Before that, the community had been called Brown’s Corner and Brown’s Mill, among other names. Elam Brown had arrived from Missouri in 1846, bought Rancho Acalanes in 1848 and founded a mill in 1853. The agricultural village became a commuter town in the mid-twentieth century. Even its pronunciation varies locally: the middle syllable can rhyme with fee, eye or pay.
